articles.title: Sensex jumps 1,200 points as crude slides below $72 and banks lead a broad rally
articles.summary: Falling oil prices eased inflation worries, pulling foreign investors back into Indian equities. Nifty closed above 23,800 for the first time in three weeks.
articles.cover_caption: Benchmark indices posted their best single-day gain in a month.
articles.body_html:
Indian shares posted their best day in a month on Tuesday as a slide in crude oil prices revived hopes of lower inflation and steady interest rates. The BSE Sensex closed 1,225 points higher at 76,917.85, while the NSE Nifty 50 ended at 23,810.85, up 1.58%.

Brent crude dropped below $72 a barrel for the first time in three weeks after major producers signalled higher output. India imports more than 85% of the oil it uses, so cheaper crude eases pressure on prices, the rupee and the government's subsidy bill.

Banks and autos lead

Banking stocks did most of the heavy lifting. The Bank Nifty gained almost 1%, with state-run lenders outperforming on hopes that falling bad loans will lift profits further. Carmakers also rallied, as lower fuel prices tend to support demand for vehicles.

Cheaper oil is the single biggest relief for the Indian market right now. It helps inflation, the currency and corporate margins at once.

Foreign institutional investors were net buyers of about ₹4,200 crore, according to provisional exchange data, reversing six weeks of steady selling.

What to watch next

  • Monthly inflation data due next week, which will shape the RBI's December decision.
  • Quarterly results from large IT and consumer companies.
  • Whether crude holds below $72 as winter demand picks up.

Analysts cautioned that a single strong session does not change the trend on its own, and advised investors to stay diversified rather than chase the rally.

articles.title: RBI holds repo rate at 5.5%, signals room for a cut if inflation keeps cooling
articles.summary: The Monetary Policy Committee voted 5-1 to keep rates unchanged, while lowering its inflation forecast for the year.
articles.body_html:
The Reserve Bank of India kept its key lending rate unchanged at 5.5% on Tuesday, but its tone suggested a cut could come as early as December if inflation keeps easing.

Five of the six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to hold the repo rate, the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. One member voted for a 0.25 percentage point cut.

Inflation forecast lowered

The central bank cut its inflation forecast for the financial year to 3.4% from 3.7%, citing a good monsoon harvest and softer global commodity prices. Retail inflation has stayed below the RBI's 4% target for four straight months.

Price stability is within reach. If the trend holds, policy has space to support growth.

What it means for you

For borrowers, home and car loan rates are unlikely to change this month. Fixed deposit rates, which several banks trimmed last week, may stay where they are until the December meeting.

Economists now expect one or two cuts before March, depending on food prices and the path of the rupee.

articles.title: Gold slips ₹1,100 from its record as the dollar steadies. Is it time to buy?
articles.summary: Jewellers report a pickup in wedding-season demand as prices cool from last week's high.
articles.body_html:
Gold prices in India eased by about ₹1,100 per 10 grams this week, slipping from last week's record as the US dollar steadied and investors booked profits.

Jewellers in Mumbai and Jaipur said the pullback has brought buyers back ahead of the wedding season, when demand usually peaks.

Should you buy now?

Financial planners generally suggest keeping gold at 5% to 10% of a portfolio, mainly as a hedge rather than a bet on short-term price moves. Buying in small amounts over time, through gold ETFs or digital gold, avoids the risk of investing everything at a peak.

Making charges and GST can add 10% or more to the cost of jewellery, so investors looking only for returns often prefer coins, bars or ETFs.

articles.title: Old or new tax regime? A simple way to decide before you file
articles.summary: Three questions about your deductions tell you which regime saves more.
articles.body_html:
Every year, salaried taxpayers in India choose between the old and new income tax regimes. The right choice depends mostly on how much you claim in deductions.

Ask yourself three questions

  • Do you pay rent and claim HRA? Large HRA claims favour the old regime.
  • Do you have a home loan? Interest deductions of up to ₹2 lakh can tip the balance.
  • Do you fill your ₹1.5 lakh Section 80C limit? If not, the new regime is often better.

If your total deductions are small, the new regime's lower rates and higher standard deduction usually mean less tax. Use your employer's calculator or the income tax portal to compare both before you file.

articles.title: India's growth story needs jobs, not just GDP headlines
articles.summary: Strong numbers mean little if young graduates can't find work that matches their skills.
articles.body_html:
India is once again the world's fastest-growing large economy. But for millions of young graduates, the headline number means little if the jobs they trained for are not there.

Growth has been led by capital-intensive sectors and services that need relatively few workers. Manufacturing, which could absorb large numbers of people, still makes up a modest share of output.

A growth story that does not create work is a story only half told.

The fix is not a single scheme. It means easier rules for small factories, better links between colleges and employers, and cities where it is affordable to live near where the jobs are. GDP will keep making headlines. Jobs should make the policy agenda.

articles.title: Explained: how a ₹5,000 monthly SIP can grow over 15 years
articles.summary: Compounding, rupee-cost averaging and why starting early matters more than timing the market.
articles.body_html:
A systematic investment plan, or SIP, lets you invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund every month. It is one of the simplest ways to build long-term wealth, because it turns saving into a habit and removes the pressure of timing the market.

How the numbers add up

Suppose you invest ₹5,000 every month for 15 years and earn an average return of 12% a year. You would put in ₹9 lakh in total, and your investment could grow to around ₹25 lakh. The extra ₹16 lakh comes from compounding: returns earning returns of their own.

Time in the market matters more than timing the market.

Why starting early matters

Stretch the same SIP to 20 years and the estimated value roughly doubles to about ₹50 lakh, even though you invest only ₹3 lakh more. That is the power of time.

Rupee-cost averaging

Because you invest the same amount every month, you buy more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high. Over time this smooths out the ups and downs of the market.

Returns from equity funds are not guaranteed and can be negative in some years. Pick funds that match your goals and how long you can stay invested, and review them once a year.
